extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, policymakers, and empirical researchers studying patent litigation outcomes
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical study classifying litigated patents by technology and industry, reporting outcome metrics (win rates, invalidity, infringement) and describing dataset construction and methodological choices for analysis of cases filed 2008–2009.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical (technology area)
rubrics_metrics.description: "An invention in which the claims cover the use of mechanical parts, either solely or predominantly, sometimes combined with heat, hydraulics, pneumatics, or other power sources or power transfer techniques."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary technology areas are mutually exclusive. Use claim language to determine classification. Mechanical patents in the dataset include inventions whose claims predominantly rely on mechanical parts and related power-transfer techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronics (technology area)
rubrics_metrics.description: "An invention in which the claims cover the use of traditional electronic circuitry or the storage or transmission of electric energy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify based on claim language indicating traditional electronic circuitry or electric-energy storage/transmission. Electronics may overlap with data-processing elements, which the authors often combine with computer-related patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemistry (technology area)
rubrics_metrics.description: "An invention in which the claims cover chemical reactions, chemical compounds with specific elements and proportions, and chemical processes specifying specific elements and amounts or proportions... includes 'small-molecule' chemistry; DNA, antibodies, and other large molecules are included in the biotechnology category instead."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include inventions claiming specific chemical components/proportions and related processes. Note that chemistry patents may also be assigned to pharmaceutical industry category; use claim content to classify technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biotechnology (technology area)
rubrics_metrics.description: "An invention in which the claims cover processes involving advanced genetic techniques intended to construct new microbial, plant, or animal strains; a product created from such a process; or the way such a process or product is used in biotechnology research."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not disaggregate genetic-engineering techniques into separate technology areas for this study. Distinguish biotechnology (as technology-scientific technique) from downstream industry uses (e.g., pharmaceuticals, medical diagnostics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Software (technology area)
rubrics_metrics.description: "An invention in which the claims cover data processing—the actual manipulation of data (and not merely transmission, receipt, or storage of data), regardless of whether the code ... is on a magnetic storage medium, embedded in a chip ('firmware'), or resident in flash memory."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify patents whose claims cover data manipulation. Exclude claims that merely cover data transmission/receipt/storage. Software is the single largest technology category in the dataset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optics (technology area)
rubrics_metrics.description: "An invention in which the claims cover the use of light waves or light energy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify based on claim coverage of light waves/energy. Optics patents in the dataset show distinct patterns (e.g., low invalidation but low infringement rates in observed outcomes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Software business method (software subset)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrow definition limited to patents "the claims of which obviously covered only such things as automated generation of customer proposals, advertising, financial techniques, the use of online catalogs."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Business-method patents are a subset of software. Do not include computer-controlled manufacturing methods. Because business-method is subset of software, it cannot be included simultaneously with the broader software category in regression models; authors ran alternative regressions where business-method and non-business-method software were mutually exclusive categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit of observation: patent-case pair
rubrics_metrics.description: "Our unit of observation is the resolution of a claim over a particular patent in a particular case (the patent-case pair)."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When cases include multiple patents, each patent outcome is a separate entry; patents litigated in multiple cases also receive separate entries. This affects counts and statistical independence considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary vs primary-plus-secondary technology coding
rubrics_metrics.description: The six primary technology areas are mutually exclusive, while the primary-plus-secondary areas are not; when both primary and secondary technology areas are included, the 949 patent-case pairs had a total of 1,244 tech areas (average 1.31 tech areas per patent-case pair).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors ran alternative specifications allowing secondary classifications; doing so increased observations (from 636 to 777 definitive outcomes) and can affect results (e.g., changing electronics win rates). Use primary-only coding for mutually exclusive analyses; allow secondary coding for sensitivity checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry category assignment procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: "Unlike technology areas, the industry categories focused more attention on the business use of the patent than on the nature of the technology itself... we paid attention to the claim language in assigning a patent to one of eleven mutually exclusive industry categories, [and] we found it necessary to focus more attention to the written description and to extrinsic evidence, especially the Internet."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign industry based on claims, written description, and extrinsic evidence about business use (web searches, marketing materials). Industry categories are mutually exclusive in the study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer & Other Electronics (industry)
rubrics_metrics.description: "This industry encompasses inventions of all kinds that purport to advance the state of the art in computing or computer device manufacturing, or to enhance users’ experiences in employing computing technology... includes software and computer hardware inventions..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors combined computer and traditional electronics because many patents include data processing elements; classify based on claims and evidence of end-use in computing or user-experience enhancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semiconductor (industry)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The semiconductor industry category includes inventions of any kind intended to advance the state of the art in researching, designing, or fabricating semiconductor chips. Technologies employed ... may include software, chemistry, optics, and mechanical."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify patents whose claims and extrinsic evidence indicate semiconductor chip research, design, or fabrication purposes, regardless of underlying technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pharmaceutical (industry)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The pharmaceutical industry category includes patents on drugs for treating diseases or other abnormal conditions in humans or animals, as well as processes for producing or using such drugs."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pharmaceutical industry patents are typically chemistry or biotechnology technologies; classify by claimed therapeutic drugs/processes and extrinsic evidence (e.g., regulatory context).

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical Devices, Methods, & Other Medical (industry)
rubrics_metrics.description: "This industry category includes non-pharmaceutical, non-biotechnology inventions of any kind used for research on, or for the diagnosis or treatment of, diseases or other abnormal conditions in humans or animals."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude pharmaceutical/process patents; include devices, diagnostic methods, and other medical technologies across various technology fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biotechnology (industry)
rubrics_metrics.description: "This category includes those inventions that are in the biotechnology technology category that do not relate to the production of pharmaceutical compositions or medical diagnostics or treatment, but that instead purport to advance the science of biotechnology itself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish biotechnology-as-industry (advances in biotech science) from pharmaceutical/medical uses; classify using claims and context of use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communications (industry)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The communications industry category includes inventions of all kinds intended to advance the state of the art in communications. Technologies represented ... include software, electronics, optics, and mechanics."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use claims and extrinsic evidence showing purpose in communications technologies or services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transportation (including automotive) (industry)
rubrics_metrics.description: "This category includes patents on any type of invention related to the production of automobiles or vehicles of any other kind intended for transporting people or cargo, and inventions related to the provision of transportation services."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include vehicle production, components, and transportation service technologies; classify by claimed usage and industry context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction (industry)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The construction industry category includes inventions of all kinds related to the erection or maintenance of structures, or to excavation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify patents whose claims pertain to structural erection/maintenance or excavation equipment/techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy (industry)
rubrics_metrics.description: "This category includes inventions of any kind associated with power generation, transportation, or consumption."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include patents whose claims or extrinsic evidence concern energy-related purposes (generation, transport, consumption).

rubrics_metrics.name: Goods & Services for Industrial & Business Uses (industry)
rubrics_metrics.description: "This category includes patents on products and services of all kinds intended for industrial and business purposes—i.e. goods and services for wholesale uses that are not in another, more specific category. Many software-implemented business method inventions are included in this category."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Catch-all for industrial/business-targeted goods/services not classified elsewhere; often includes business-method software when deployed for business uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goods & Services for Consumer Uses (industry)
rubrics_metrics.description: "This category includes patents on products and services of all kinds intended for personal consumer purposes—i.e. goods and services for retail uses that are not in another, more specific category. Many software-implemented business method inventions are included in this category."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify patents targeted at retail/consumer use not otherwise categorized; use product/service market evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset temporal scope limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Our data set is limited to lawsuits filed in 2008 and 2009... The exact beginning and ending points of our dataset—January 1, 2008 and December 31, 2009—are artificial cutoffs."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the sample is a snapshot; findings may differ outside these filing dates due to subsequent legal developments (e.g., AIA, Therasense, subject-matter case law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection limitation: only adjudicated merits decisions included
rubrics_metrics.description: "Our data set only contains patents that were subject to a ruling on summary judgment, a trial, or an appeal... most lawsuits settle, and ... cases that settled before any substantive patent ruling are completely absent from our data set."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Results are not generalizable to all filed suits or to settled/abandoned disputes. Be cautious about direction of settlement-selection bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset size and statistical power caution
rubrics_metrics.description: "The size of our dataset is relatively modest, with fewer than 1,000 patent observations... once the dataset is broken down by technology and further still by patent law doctrine, the number of observations in each category becomes much smaller, making statistical significance harder to find."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret subgroup statistics cautiously; small cell counts can yield unstable estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of statistical model and clustering
rubrics_metrics.description: "We used logistic regression (or logit) models, because each of our dependent variables (specific outcomes) is binary (or 'dummy'—'yes' or 'no'). ... To account for the lack of complete independence among observations, we clustered on the standard errors of the unique patent numbers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use logit for binary outcomes and cluster standard errors by patent to address correlated observations (same patent litigated multiple times; multiple patents in same case; consolidated cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Regression specification constraint for software/business-method categories
rubrics_metrics.description: "Because the business method category is a subset of software generally, it cannot be included in multiple regressions that also include the broader software category. We did, however, run some regressions including software business method and software non-business method patents as mutually exclusive categories that substitute for the broader software category."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modeling technology effects, avoid collinearity by not including both a superset (software) and its subset (business-method) simultaneously; consider alternative mutually exclusive coding schemes for sensitivity analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome metric: definitive win rate (by technology/industry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitive win rate is the proportion of patent-case pairs that resulted in the patent owner prevailing in a definitive outcome (trial, summary judgment, or appeal). Example: overall patentees won 26% of cases that went to a definitive outcome; by technology chemistry = 52.1%, software = 13.1%, biotech = 8.1%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute conditioning on cases that reached a definitive decision; exclude cases that settled before merits ruling. Report by technology and industry to reveal systematic differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome metric: invalidity rate (by technology/industry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Invalidity rate measures proportion of decisions on validity where the patent was held invalid (any stage). Example: overall ~43% of patents that went to final judgment on validity were invalidated; technology-specific rates vary (e.g., biotech 80%, chemistry 25.6%, optics 21.4%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report invalidity rates conditional on resolution of validity dispute. Break out by statutory grounds (102, 103, 112) for more granular analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome metric: infringement rate (by technology/industry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement rate measures proportion of decisions on infringement where infringement was found (literal or DOE). Example: chemistry infringement rate 68.4%, software 19.2%, optics 15.0%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Condition on cases that resolved infringement disputes. Present separate statistics for business-method vs non-business-method software when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome metric: summary-judgment invalidity win rate (by technology)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion of summary-judgment motions for invalidity granted by technology. Example: higher summary-judgment grant rates for biotech and software (especially business-method patents) than for some other technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to analyze procedural posture differences; note that summary-judgment wins count as definitive wins for defendants. Compare across technologies to detect differences in courts' willingness to grant SJ invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity grounds taxonomy (102, 103, 112 categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Invalidity arguments are categorized by common statutory grounds: 102 (prior art/novelty), 103 (obviousness), 112(b) indefiniteness, and 112 enablement/written-description failures. The study reports win rates on each by technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break invalidity outcomes down by statutory ground to identify technology-specific vulnerabilities (e.g., software/electronics more vulnerable to indefiniteness; biotech/mechanical more to enablement/written description).
